issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette:
Kwame is a 19-year-old UX designer living in a mid-sized American city. He was born in Ghana and came to the United States with his family when he was twelve. He is single and lives alone in a small apartment near the tech incubator where he works. He sought therapy six months after the end of a stalking episode that lasted nearly four months.

The stalking began when a former coworker, a woman in her late twenties named Elena, started sending him long, rambling emails after he declined her invitation to coffee. At first, Kwame ignored them. But the messages escalated quickly: dozens of texts per night, voicemails at 2 a.m., and finally, appearances outside his office building and his apartment. She would wait in the lobby, or stand across the street, watching. He changed his route to work three times, but she always found him. The police took a report but said there was not enough evidence for a restraining order. The worst night came when he found her sitting on the steps of his building, holding a photograph of the two of them she had taken without his knowledge. He moved out of his apartment the next day and stayed with a friend for two weeks. Elena was eventually arrested for trespassing at his office, but by then Kwame had already resigned from the job he loved.

In the months that followed, Kwame came to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous. He had always considered himself a careful person, but now he saw threats everywhere. He stopped going to coffee shops, avoided crowded sidewalks, and began checking the locks on his door three times before bed. He was certain that if he let his guard down for even a moment, something terrible would happen. He told his therapist, "I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next." This constant vigilance exhausted him, but he could not imagine relaxing it. He also blamed himself for the stalking. In quiet moments, he replayed the initial interaction with Elena, wondering if he had been too friendly, too polite, too accommodating. He told himself that the event happened because of the way he acted, and that if he had been firmer from the start, none of it would have unfolded. This self-blame sat heavily in his chest, separate from the fear but adding its own weight.

At work, Kwame's vigilance affected his performance. He sat with his back to the wall in every meeting, and he could not focus when colleagues approached his desk from behind. He began working from home as often as possible, telling his manager he was more productive in a quiet space. In truth, he was afraid of who might walk through the office door. He had stopped going to the gym, stopped seeing friends, and stopped dating. He felt trapped in a small, watchful life.

What finally brought Kwame to therapy was a panic attack in a grocery store. A woman in the produce aisle had been staring at him-or he thought she was staring-and he had frozen, heart hammering, unable to move until she walked away. He realized he could not keep living this way. He was afraid of the world, and he was afraid of himself for having been, as he saw it, the cause of his own suffering. He wanted to stop checking locks, stop scanning every face, stop replaying that first conversation. He wanted to feel safe, but he did not know what that would even feel like anymore.
